sections.name: The Pentateuch
sections.summary: The Pentateuch (Greek for 'five scrolls'), called the Torah ('instruction') in Judaism, runs from creation to Israel camped on the edge of the promised land. Everything after it rests on these books: who God is, what has gone wrong with the world, God's promise to Abraham, the rescue from Egypt, and the covenant at Sinai that shaped Israel's worship and life. About half is story and half is law.
sections.reading: Read it as a story with laws inside it. The commandments were given to a people God had already rescued; obedience is the response to grace, not the way to earn it.

sections.name: The Historical Books
sections.summary: Twelve books covering roughly a thousand years, from Israel entering Canaan (about 1400 BC on the traditional dating) to Jerusalem rebuilt after the exile (about 430 BC). They trace the conquest, the chaos of the judges, the rise of the kingdom under Saul, David and Solomon, its split into north and south, the fall of both to Assyria and Babylon, and the return home. In the Hebrew Bible, Joshua to Kings are called the 'Former Prophets'.
sections.reading: This is history written to teach. The writers judge each period by faithfulness to God, especially by the standards of Deuteronomy. Chronicles retells Samuel and Kings for the returned exiles, so where they overlap, read them side by side.

sections.name: Wisdom and Poetry
sections.summary: Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs turn from Israel's national story to the life of a person before God: how to live wisely, how to pray in pain and in joy, how to face suffering, death and love. They are written mostly in Hebrew poetry.
sections.reading: Hebrew poetry rhymes ideas rather than sounds: the second line repeats, sharpens or contrasts the first. Proverbs describes how life usually works, not guarantees; Job and Ecclesiastes deal honestly with the exceptions.

sections.name: The Major Prophets
sections.summary: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel and Daniel are 'major' because they are long, not because they matter more. They span about 740 to 530 BC: Assyria's threat, Babylon's conquest of Jerusalem, and the exile. The prophets were covenant messengers more than fortune-tellers. They called God's people back, announced judgment, and held out hope beyond it: a new covenant, a coming king, and a renewed creation.
sections.reading: Much of it is poetry and arranged by theme, not date, so it helps to know which king or crisis a passage addresses. Most prophecies spoke first to their own day, even when they also reach further.

sections.name: The Minor Prophets
sections.summary: Twelve shorter books, kept on one scroll in the Hebrew Bible. They range from about 800 BC to about 430 BC and aren't in strict date order. Hosea, Amos, Jonah and Micah belong to the Assyrian period; Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah and probably Obadiah to Babylon's rise; Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi to the years after the exile.
sections.reading: Recurring threads run through all twelve: the day of the LORD, justice for the poor, empty worship versus true devotion, and God's mercy to those who return to him. Reading them in historical order alongside Kings and Ezra-Nehemiah brings them to life.

sections.name: The Gospels
sections.summary: Four accounts of Jesus' life, death and resurrection. 'Gospel' means 'good news'. Matthew, Mark and Luke are called the Synoptic Gospels ('seen together') because they share much material and order; John goes his own way. Each is a portrait for a particular audience: Matthew shows Jesus as Israel's Messiah, Mark the suffering Son of God, Luke the Savior of all people, John the eternal Word made flesh.
sections.reading: They are ancient biographies, selecting and arranging events to make a point rather than keeping strict chronology. When the same story appears in more than one Gospel, notice what each writer chooses to emphasize.

sections.name: History of the Church
sections.summary: Acts is the only book of its kind in the New Testament: the church's first thirty years, from Jesus' ascension (about AD 30) to Paul under house arrest in Rome (about AD 62). It follows the gospel outward from Jerusalem to Rome and from Jews to Gentiles.
sections.reading: Acts is the setting for most of the letters. When you read a letter of Paul's, look up when he was in that city in Acts.

sections.name: Paul's Letters
sections.summary: Thirteen letters from the apostle Paul, a former persecutor of the church who became its missionary to the Gentiles. Nine are to churches and four to individuals. They are arranged roughly by length, not date: the earliest are probably Galatians and 1 Thessalonians (about AD 49–51), the last 2 Timothy (about AD 67).
sections.reading: These are real letters to real situations, so read each one asking what was happening on the other end. Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon were written from prison; 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus are called the Pastoral Letters.

sections.name: The General Letters
sections.summary: Hebrews, James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1, 2 and 3 John, and Jude. Most are addressed to wide audiences rather than one church, which is why they're called general (or 'catholic', meaning universal) letters. Apart from Hebrews, they are named after their authors rather than their readers.
sections.reading: Their shared concerns: holding on under pressure, faith that shows itself in action, living as outsiders in society, and guarding the truth against false teachers.

sections.name: Prophecy
sections.summary: Revelation is apocalyptic prophecy, a kind of writing built from visions and symbols also found in Daniel, Ezekiel and Zechariah. It was written to seven real churches in Asia Minor, and its images draw heavily on the Old Testament.
sections.reading: Christians read it in four main ways: as mostly about the first century (preterist), as a map of church history (historicist), as mainly about the end of the age (futurist), or as timeless pictures of the battle between good and evil (idealist). All agree on its center: the Lamb who was slain is on the throne and wins.

books.means: Greek for 'origin' or 'beginning'. The Hebrew title, Bereshit, is its first word: 'In the beginning'.
books.author: Moses (traditional)
books.authorMeans: Hebrew Mosheh sounds like 'to draw out' (Exodus 2:10); it is probably also an Egyptian name meaning 'son' or 'born of'.
books.authorNote: The books of the Pentateuch don't name their author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and Jesus himself, speak of them as 'the Law of Moses', but some details were added later, such as the account of Moses' death. Many scholars hold that the books were compiled from several sources over centuries, reaching final form after the exile.
books.date: About 1446–1406 BC, in the wilderness years (later if the Exodus is dated about 1260 BC)
books.to: Israel, on the way from Egypt to Canaan
books.covers: From creation to the death of Joseph in Egypt
books.summary: Genesis answers Israel's first questions: who made the world, why it is broken, and why God chose one family. Chapters 1–11 sweep from creation through the fall, the flood and the tower of Babel, each episode ending in judgment tempered by mercy. Chapters 12–50 slow down to follow four generations, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, to whom God promises land, descendants and blessing for all nations. Those promises are tested by barrenness, deceit, famine and family betrayal, and the book closes with Israel's family alive in Egypt because of Joseph, still waiting for the land.
themes: Creation: one God makes a good world by his word
Sin spreads from Eden to Babel
Providence: 'You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good' (50:20)
books.fits: The foundation for everything after it. The promise to Abraham drives the rest of the Old Testament, and the New Testament reads Christ as Abraham's offspring through whom all nations are blessed (Galatians 3:8, 16). Paul's 'last Adam' (Romans 5) and Revelation's new creation both look back here.

books.means: Greek for 'going out'. The Hebrew title, Shemot, means 'Names', from its opening words.
books.author: Moses (traditional)
books.authorMeans: Hebrew Mosheh sounds like 'to draw out' (Exodus 2:10); it is probably also an Egyptian name meaning 'son' or 'born of'.
books.authorNote: The books of the Pentateuch don't name their author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and Jesus himself, speak of them as 'the Law of Moses', but some details were added later, such as the account of Moses' death. Many scholars hold that the books were compiled from several sources over centuries, reaching final form after the exile.
books.covers: From Israel's slavery in Egypt to the tabernacle at Mount Sinai
books.summary: Exodus moves from slavery to worship. A new Pharaoh enslaves Jacob's descendants, and God calls Moses at the burning bush, reveals his name, and breaks Egypt's power through ten plagues. The Passover and the crossing of the sea become Israel's defining rescue. At Sinai God makes a covenant with the nation and gives the Ten Commandments and the laws that follow. After the golden calf nearly ends it all, God renews the covenant and comes to live among his people: in the last chapter his glory fills the tabernacle.
themes: Redemption: God rescues a people for himself
God's name and presence: 'I AM WHO I AM' (3:14)
The tabernacle: God dwelling with his people
books.fits: The Old Testament's great act of salvation, recalled again and again by psalms and prophets. Jesus died at Passover, Paul calls him 'our Passover lamb' (1 Corinthians 5:7), and John says the Word 'made his dwelling' (literally 'tabernacled') among us (John 1:14).

books.means: From Greek and Latin, 'about the Levites', Israel's priestly tribe. The Hebrew title, Vayikra, means 'And he called'.
books.kind: Law: instructions for worship and holiness
books.author: Moses (traditional)
books.authorMeans: Hebrew Mosheh sounds like 'to draw out' (Exodus 2:10); it is probably also an Egyptian name meaning 'son' or 'born of'.
books.authorNote: The books of the Pentateuch don't name their author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and Jesus himself, speak of them as 'the Law of Moses', but some details were added later, such as the account of Moses' death. Many scholars hold that the books were compiled from several sources over centuries, reaching final form after the exile.
books.covers: About one month at Mount Sinai
books.summary: Leviticus answers the question Exodus leaves open: how can a holy God live among sinful people? It sets out the offerings (1–7), the ordination of the priests (8–10), the laws of clean and unclean (11–15), and the Day of Atonement (16), when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place to make atonement for the people. The 'Holiness Code' (17–27) then carries holiness into everyday life: family, food, justice, festivals and the land, summed up in 'Love your neighbor as yourself' (19:18).
themes: Holiness: 'Be holy, because I am holy' (11:44)
books.fits: The book of Hebrews is largely a commentary on Leviticus, presenting Jesus as both the high priest and the sacrifice the offerings pointed to (Hebrews 9–10). Jesus called Leviticus 19:18 the second greatest commandment.

books.means: Named for the two censuses of Israel (chapters 1 and 26). The Hebrew title, Bemidbar, means 'In the wilderness'.
books.kind: Narrative history, law and census records
books.author: Moses (traditional)
books.authorMeans: Hebrew Mosheh sounds like 'to draw out' (Exodus 2:10); it is probably also an Egyptian name meaning 'son' or 'born of'.
books.authorNote: The books of the Pentateuch don't name their author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and Jesus himself, speak of them as 'the Law of Moses', but some details were added later, such as the account of Moses' death. Many scholars hold that the books were compiled from several sources over centuries, reaching final form after the exile.
books.to: The new generation about to enter Canaan
books.covers: About 38 years, from Sinai to the plains of Moab
books.summary: Numbers follows Israel from Sinai to the edge of Canaan, a journey of weeks that took nearly forty years. After the tribes are counted and organized, the people set out, but grumbling turns into rebellion when they refuse to enter the land at Kadesh (13–14). That generation dies in the wilderness. Along the way come Korah's revolt, Moses' own failure at Meribah, the bronze snake, and Balaam, who is hired to curse Israel and can only bless. A second census counts the new generation, ready on the plains of Moab.
themes: God's faithfulness to an unfaithful people
A new generation and a second chance
books.fits: Psalm 95 and Hebrews 3–4 use the wilderness generation as a warning against hardened hearts, and Paul says these things 'were written down as warnings for us' (1 Corinthians 10:11). Jesus compared his being lifted up on the cross to the bronze snake (John 3:14).

books.means: Greek for 'second law', since Moses restates the law. The Hebrew title, Devarim, means 'Words'.
books.kind: Sermons, shaped like an ancient covenant treaty
books.author: Moses (traditional)
books.authorMeans: Hebrew Mosheh sounds like 'to draw out' (Exodus 2:10); it is probably also an Egyptian name meaning 'son' or 'born of'.
books.authorNote: The book presents itself as Moses' speeches; the account of his death (chapter 34) was added by someone else. Many scholars connect the book's final form with King Josiah's reforms in the 600s BC (2 Kings 22).
books.to: The generation about to enter Canaan
books.covers: About a month on the plains of Moab, ending with Moses' death
books.summary: Deuteronomy is Moses' farewell: three sermons to the generation about to enter Canaan. He retells their history, repeats and applies the law for life in the land, and calls them to love the LORD with all their heart. The book is shaped like an ancient treaty between a great king and his people, with history, terms, blessings and curses, and witnesses. It ends with Moses' song and blessing, his view of the land from Mount Nebo, and his death.
themes: Love and loyalty to the one God (the Shema, 6:4–5)
Remember: don't forget what God has done
outline: Second sermon: the law for life in the land
books.fits: The lens for the historical books, which judge Israel by its standards. Jesus answered each of Satan's temptations with a verse from Deuteronomy (Matthew 4) and named 6:5 the greatest commandment.

books.means: Named after its main character.
books.author: Unknown; Jewish tradition says Joshua, with later additions
books.authorMeans: Hebrew Yehoshua, 'the LORD saves'. It is the same name as Jesus (Greek Iesous).
books.date: Events about 1406–1375 BC (traditional); written soon after
books.covers: Israel's entry into Canaan and the division of the land
books.summary: Joshua tells how Israel entered and settled the land promised to Abraham. Under Moses' successor the people cross the Jordan, see Jericho's walls fall, and suffer defeat at Ai because of Achan's sin. Campaigns in the south and north break the main Canaanite resistance, though much land is still left to take. The second half divides the land among the tribes and sets up cities of refuge. Joshua ends with a covenant renewal at Shechem: 'As for me and my household, we will serve the LORD.'
themes: Holiness and judgment in the conquest
books.fits: Fulfills the promises of Genesis and Deuteronomy. Hebrews notes that Joshua's 'rest' wasn't the final one (Hebrews 4:8). Rahab of Jericho appears in Jesus' family line (Matthew 1:5) and in the list of the faithful (Hebrews 11:31).

books.means: Named for the leaders (Hebrew shophetim) God raised up to rescue Israel; they were more military deliverers than courtroom judges.
books.author: Unknown; Jewish tradition says Samuel
books.date: Events about 1375–1050 BC; written early in the monarchy (it says 'In those days Israel had no king')
books.covers: From Joshua's death to just before Samuel
books.summary: Judges shows what happens when Israel forgets God after Joshua. A cycle repeats: the people turn to idols, God hands them over to oppressors, they cry out, and God raises a deliverer: Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson and others. Each round grows darker, and the deliverers themselves become more flawed. The last chapters show Israel's collapse from within, with idolatry, the horrific crime at Gibeah and civil war, under the refrain 'everyone did as they saw fit.'
themes: Flawed leaders and the need for a true king
books.fits: The bridge between Joshua and the kings, showing why Israel wanted a king. Ruth is set in the same period. Hebrews 11 names Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah among those who acted in faith.

books.means: Named after Ruth, whose name may mean 'friend' or 'companion'.
books.author: Unknown; Jewish tradition says Samuel
books.date: Set in the time of the judges; written during or after David's reign, since it ends with his family tree
books.summary: A famine sends Naomi's family from Bethlehem to Moab, where her husband and both sons die. Her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth refuses to leave her: 'Your people will be my people and your God my God.' Back in Bethlehem, Ruth gleans in the fields of Boaz, a relative, who acts as kinsman-redeemer, marries her and restores Naomi's family. Their son Obed becomes the grandfather of King David.
books.fits: A ray of faithfulness in the dark days of the judges, leading to David. Ruth is one of four women named in Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:5).

books.means: Named after Samuel, the prophet who anointed Israel's first two kings. 1 and 2 Samuel were originally one book.
books.author: Unknown; it draws on records by Samuel, Nathan and Gad (1 Chronicles 29:29)
books.authorMeans: Samuel probably means 'name of God' or 'heard by God' (1 Samuel 1:20).
books.date: Events about 1100–1010 BC; compiled after the kingdom divided in 930 BC
books.summary: First Samuel tells how Israel got a king. Barren Hannah prays for a son and gives Samuel to the LORD; he grows up to be prophet and judge as Eli's priestly family falls and the ark is captured. The people demand a king 'like all the nations', and God gives them Saul, tall and impressive but disobedient. God rejects Saul and has Samuel anoint the shepherd boy David, who kills Goliath and then spends years on the run from Saul's jealousy, refusing to harm 'the LORD's anointed'. The book ends with Saul's death on Mount Gilboa.
themes: God lifts up the humble (Hannah's song, 2:1–10)
What kind of king Israel needs
To obey is better than sacrifice (15:22)
The LORD looks at the heart (16:7)
books.fits: With 2 Samuel, the hinge from the judges to the kings. David becomes the model king and the root of the hope for a Messiah. Mary's song (Luke 1:46–55) echoes Hannah's.

books.means: See 1 Samuel; the two were originally one book.
books.author: Unknown; it draws on records by Samuel, Nathan and Gad (1 Chronicles 29:29)
books.date: Events about 1010–970 BC (David's reign); compiled after 930 BC
books.summary: Second Samuel is the story of David's reign. He becomes king over Judah, then over all Israel, captures Jerusalem and brings the ark there. In chapter 7 God promises David a 'house': a dynasty and a kingdom that will last forever. Victories follow, then David's adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of her husband Uriah. The prophet Nathan confronts him and David repents, but the sword never leaves his house: Amnon's crime, Absalom's revolt and death, and further rebellion. The book closes with David's songs and last words.
themes: Sin has consequences even when forgiven
books.fits: God's covenant with David is the backbone of the promise of a Messiah; the New Testament opens by calling Jesus 'the son of David' (Matthew 1:1). Psalm 51 comes out of chapters 11–12.

books.means: Named for its subject, the kings of Israel and Judah. 1 and 2 Kings were originally one book.
books.author: Unknown; Jewish tradition says Jeremiah
books.date: Events about 970–850 BC; the whole work was finished during the exile (after 561 BC)
books.summary: First Kings begins in glory and ends in division. Solomon asks for wisdom, builds the temple, and Israel reaches its height, but his many foreign wives turn his heart to other gods. After his death the kingdom splits: ten northern tribes (Israel) under Jeroboam, who sets up golden calves, and Judah in the south under David's line. The second half centers on Elijah's battle against Baal worship under King Ahab and Queen Jezebel: the drought, fire from heaven on Mount Carmel, and the gentle whisper at Horeb.
themes: The nation's fate follows its faithfulness
The power of the prophetic word
books.fits: 1 and 2 Kings explain, in light of Deuteronomy, why Israel ended in exile. Jesus pointed to Solomon's splendor and to Elijah's ministry to a foreign widow (Matthew 6:29; Luke 4:25–26).

books.means: See 1 Kings; the two were originally one book.
books.author: Unknown; Jewish tradition says Jeremiah
books.date: Events about 850–561 BC; finished during the exile
books.summary: Second Kings carries both kingdoms to their end. Elisha succeeds Elijah with miracles of mercy and judgment. The northern kingdom, never free of Jeroboam's sins, falls to Assyria in 722 BC, and chapter 17 explains why. Judah lasts longer, with reforming kings like Hezekiah, who sees Jerusalem saved from the Assyrian Sennacherib, and Josiah, who rediscovers the Book of the Law. But Manasseh's evil has sealed Judah's fate: Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC. The last scene, King Jehoiachin released from prison in Babylon, leaves a thin thread of hope for David's line.
themes: The power of God's word through the prophets
books.fits: The background to most of the prophets: Hosea and Amos in the north, Isaiah with Hezekiah, Jeremiah in Judah's last days. The exile it ends with sets the stage for Daniel, Ezra and Nehemiah.

books.means: From the Greek and Latin titles; the Hebrew title means 'The events of the days'. 1 and 2 Chronicles were originally one book.
books.author: Unknown, often called 'the Chronicler'; Jewish tradition says Ezra
books.to: Jews who had returned from exile
books.covers: Genealogies from Adam, then the reign of David
books.summary: Chronicles retells Israel's history for the Jews who had come back from exile and were rebuilding. First Chronicles opens with nine chapters of genealogies from Adam to the returned exiles, tying the small community to the whole story of God's people. It then turns to David, leaving out his sin with Bathsheba and Absalom's revolt, and focuses on his bringing the ark to Jerusalem, God's covenant with him, and his careful preparations for the temple and its worship.
themes: The returned community is still God's Israel
Worship and the temple at the center
books.fits: Parallels Samuel and Kings but writes for a different moment: to encourage, not to explain the exile. Chronicles is the last book of the Hebrew Bible, so Jesus' 'from Abel to Zechariah' (Luke 11:51) may span the whole Old Testament.

books.means: See 1 Chronicles; the two were originally one book.
books.author: Unknown, often called 'the Chronicler'; Jewish tradition says Ezra
books.to: Jews who had returned from exile
books.covers: From Solomon to Cyrus' decree in 538 BC
books.summary: Second Chronicles follows Judah alone from Solomon's temple to the exile. It dwells on the temple's building and dedication, then measures each king by how he treated true worship. Reformers like Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah get long chapters, and even the wicked Manasseh repents. The theme is 7:14: when God's people humble themselves and seek him, he hears. The book ends not in ruin but with Cyrus' decree letting the exiles go home to rebuild.
books.fits: Its hopeful ending sets up Ezra and Nehemiah, which pick up the story at Cyrus' decree.

books.means: Named after Ezra. Ezra and Nehemiah were originally one book.
books.kind: Narrative history with records and memoirs
books.author: Ezra (traditional); parts are in his own first-person voice
books.authorMeans: Ezra means 'help'.
books.summary: Ezra tells of two returns from Babylon. In the first (1–6), Zerubbabel leads about 50,000 exiles home under Cyrus' decree. They rebuild the altar and lay the temple's foundation, but opposition halts the work until, urged on by Haggai and Zechariah, they finish it in 516 BC. Nearly sixty years later (7–10), Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law, arrives with a second group, devoted 'to the study and observance of the Law of the LORD, and to teaching' it. He confronts marriages with the surrounding peoples, and the community confesses and separates.
themes: God moves kings to keep his word
outline: The first return and the temple
books.fits: Fulfills Jeremiah's promise of return after seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10). Read alongside Haggai and Zechariah, who preached during chapters 5–6.

books.means: Named after Nehemiah.
books.author: Nehemiah's own memoirs, joined with Ezra's material
books.authorMeans: Nehemiah means 'the LORD comforts'.
books.summary: Nehemiah, cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes, hears that Jerusalem's walls are still in ruins. After praying, he gets leave to go, and despite mockery, threats and plots he leads the people to rebuild the wall in 52 days. Ezra then reads the Law aloud to the gathered people, who weep, celebrate, confess their history and sign a covenant. Nehemiah repopulates the city and dedicates the wall, but on a second visit finds the people slipping back, and confronts them again.
books.fits: The last historical events of the Old Testament. Malachi preaches against the same failures. The rebuilt city and temple are the ones Jesus later walked in.

books.means: Named after Esther, a Persian name probably meaning 'star'. Her Hebrew name, Hadassah, means 'myrtle'.
books.author: Unknown
books.date: Events about 483–473 BC under Xerxes I; written in the Persian period
books.to: Jews, explaining the feast of Purim
books.summary: Esther is set in the Persian court among Jews who stayed in exile. King Xerxes deposes his queen and chooses Esther, a young Jewish woman raised by her cousin Mordecai, who keeps her background secret. When the official Haman plots to wipe out all the Jews, Mordecai tells Esther she may have come to her position 'for such a time as this.' Risking her life, she goes to the king. Haman is hanged on his own gallows and the Jews are allowed to defend themselves. The feast of Purim remembers the deliverance.
themes: Providence where God is never named
Reversal: the proud fall, the humble rise
books.fits: God is never mentioned, yet his hidden hand is everywhere. It shows God preserving the people through whom the Messiah would come.

books.means: Named after Job, whose name may mean 'where is the father?' or 'persecuted one'.
books.kind: Wisdom literature: poetry framed by a prose story
books.author: Unknown
books.date: Unknown. The setting feels patriarchal (wealth in flocks, Job offering his own sacrifices); proposals for the writing range from Solomon's time to the exile
books.summary: Job is a blameless man who loses his wealth, his children and his health after God allows Satan to test whether he serves God for nothing. Three friends come to comfort him, then argue at length that suffering must be punishment for sin. Job insists on his innocence and demands a hearing with God. A younger man, Elihu, speaks next. At last God answers out of the storm, not with an explanation but with a tour of creation that displays his wisdom and power. Job repents of speaking beyond his knowledge, God rebukes the friends, and Job's fortunes are restored.
books.fits: Pushes back against the simple formula that the righteous always prosper, which Proverbs can seem to suggest. James points to Job's perseverance (James 5:11).

books.means: From Greek psalmoi, songs sung to a stringed instrument. The Hebrew title, Tehillim, means 'Praises'.
books.author: Many: David (73 psalms carry his name), Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon, Moses (Psalm 90), and many unnamed
books.authorMeans: David means 'beloved'.
books.date: From about Moses' time (Psalm 90) to after the exile (Psalm 137); gathered into its final form after the exile
books.to: Israel at worship, and every believer at prayer
books.summary: Psalms is Israel's prayer book and hymnbook: 150 poems for every condition of the soul. Laments, the most common kind, pour out fear, anger and grief, yet nearly always turn to trust. Hymns praise God as creator and king; thanksgiving psalms remember specific rescues; royal psalms celebrate the king God has anointed; wisdom psalms contrast two ways of life. The collection is arranged in five books, each ending with a short burst of praise, and it moves overall from lament toward praise, closing with five hallelujah psalms.
themes: The anointed king and the Messiah
books.fits: The Old Testament book most quoted in the New. Jesus prayed Psalms 22 and 31 on the cross, and the apostles read Psalms 2, 16 and 110 as pointing to him.

books.means: The Hebrew title, Mishlei, means 'sayings' or 'comparisons'.
books.author: Mainly Solomon, with sayings of 'the wise', proverbs copied by Hezekiah's men (25:1), Agur (30) and King Lemuel (31)
books.authorMeans: Solomon comes from shalom, 'peace'.
books.date: Solomon's material about 970–930 BC; the collection completed after Hezekiah (about 700 BC)
books.to: Young people, and anyone who wants to live wisely
books.summary: Proverbs teaches skill for living in God's world. The first nine chapters are a father's talks to his son, setting Lady Wisdom against the seductive woman Folly and calling the young to choose wisdom's path. The rest are short sayings, mostly two lines each, about speech, work, money, friendship, anger, marriage and justice. They are observations about how life usually goes, not promises without exceptions. The book ends with a portrait of 'a wife of noble character', wisdom lived out.
themes: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (1:7)
books.fits: Practical godliness for daily life. The New Testament calls Christ the one 'in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom' (Colossians 2:3), and James is its closest cousin.

books.means: Greek for 'one who addresses an assembly', translating the Hebrew Qoheleth, 'the Teacher' or 'the Preacher'.
books.author: Qoheleth, 'son of David, king in Jerusalem': traditionally Solomon
books.authorMeans: Qoheleth means 'one who gathers' people or sayings.
books.authorNote: Many scholars think a later writer took on Solomon's voice, because of the book's language and outlook. The book never actually names Solomon.
books.date: About 935 BC if by Solomon; otherwise the 400s to 200s BC
books.summary: The Teacher sets out to find what lasts 'under the sun' and tries everything: wisdom, pleasure, building, wealth, work. His verdict: 'Meaningless! Everything is meaningless.' The Hebrew word, hebel, means vapor or breath, something fleeting and beyond our grasp. Death erases the difference between the wise and the fool, and the world is full of injustice. Yet again and again he commends receiving food, work and love as gifts from God, and he ends: 'Fear God and keep his commandments.'
themes: Living in the fear of God
outline: Time and the limits of life
books.fits: A counterweight to easy answers. Paul's 'the creation was subjected to frustration' (Romans 8:20) uses the same Greek word the old translation used for hebel, and the resurrection answers the Teacher's 'under the sun'.

books.means: The Hebrew 'Song of Songs' means 'the greatest song'. It is also called the Song of Solomon.
books.author: 'Solomon's' (1:1), which can mean by, for or about him
books.authorMeans: Solomon comes from shalom, 'peace'.
books.date: 10th century BC if by Solomon; some scholars date it later
books.summary: The Song of Songs is a series of love poems in which a young woman and her beloved speak to and about each other, with a chorus of 'daughters of Jerusalem'. It celebrates desire, beauty, longing, absence and reunion, and the faithful commitment of marriage, in vivid images of gardens, vineyards and countryside. The woman speaks more than anyone else. Its high point: 'love is as strong as death… Many waters cannot quench love.'
themes: Desire and patience: 'do not arouse love until it so desires'
A picture of God's love for his people
books.fits: Read plainly, it celebrates human love as part of God's good creation. Jewish and Christian readers have also long read it as a picture of God and Israel, or Christ and the church (compare Ephesians 5:31–32).

books.means: Named after the prophet Isaiah.
books.author: Isaiah son of Amoz, who prophesied in Jerusalem about 740–681 BC
books.authorMeans: Isaiah means 'the LORD is salvation'.
books.authorNote: Many scholars assign chapters 40–66 to one or more later prophets writing during or after the exile, because those chapters address the exiles and name Cyrus. The New Testament quotes both halves under Isaiah's name (John 12:38–41).
books.to: Judah and Jerusalem, and later generations in exile
books.summary: Isaiah preached in Jerusalem under four kings as Assyria swallowed nation after nation. Chapters 1–39 call Judah to trust God rather than military alliances, announce judgment on Judah and the nations, and promise a coming king: Immanuel, a child called 'Mighty God', a shoot from the stump of Jesse. Hezekiah's rescue from Sennacherib closes this half. Chapters 40–66 open with 'Comfort, comfort my people' and look beyond the Babylonian exile to the return under Cyrus, to the Servant of the LORD who suffers for others (52:13–53:12), and to new heavens and a new earth.
themes: The coming king and the Suffering Servant
books.fits: Sometimes called 'the fifth gospel', it is quoted in the New Testament more than any other prophet. Jesus began his ministry by reading Isaiah 61 (Luke 4:18–21), and Isaiah 53 is the clearest Old Testament picture of his death for sin.

books.means: Named after the prophet Jeremiah.
books.author: Jeremiah, with his scribe Baruch (chapter 36)
books.authorMeans: Jeremiah probably means 'the LORD exalts' or 'the LORD establishes'.
books.to: Judah in its last years, and the first exiles
books.summary: Jeremiah was called as a young man and preached for about forty years under Judah's last five kings, warning that Babylon would come unless the people repented. He was rejected, beaten, imprisoned and thrown into a cistern; he lamented his calling yet couldn't keep the word in (20:9). He saw Jerusalem fall in 586 BC and was taken to Egypt against his will. Amid the judgment comes the promise of a new covenant written on hearts (31:31–34) and return after seventy years. The book is arranged more by theme than by date.
outline: Conflict with leaders and false prophets
books.fits: Jesus inaugurated the new covenant of chapter 31 at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20), and Hebrews 8 quotes it in full.

books.means: The Hebrew title, Ekah, is its first word: 'How!', a cry of grief.
books.author: Unknown; tradition says Jeremiah
books.date: Soon after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC
books.to: Survivors of the fall of Jerusalem
books.summary: Five poems of grief over Jerusalem's destruction by Babylon. Four are acrostics, each verse or stanza beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, as if giving grief an order from A to Z. The city is pictured as a widow with no one to comfort her. The poet admits the disaster was deserved, but at the center of the book faith breaks through: 'his compassions never fail. They are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.' The last poem is a prayer that ends with an open question.
outline: Hope in the midst of suffering
books.fits: Shows that lament is a form of faith. Jews still read it each year on the 9th of Av, mourning the destruction of the temple.

books.means: Named after the prophet Ezekiel.
books.author: Ezekiel, a priest taken to Babylon in 597 BC
books.authorMeans: Ezekiel means 'God strengthens'.
books.summary: Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon with the first exiles, where he saw an overwhelming vision of God's glory by the Kebar River. Before Jerusalem fell he preached judgment through visions and strange sign-acts (lying on his side for months, shaving his head) and saw the glory of God leave the temple. After the fall his message turned to hope: God will give a new heart and spirit, be Israel's shepherd himself, and breathe life into a valley of dry bones. The book ends with a vision of a new temple with a river of life flowing from it, and a city named 'The LORD is there'.
books.fits: Jesus' 'I am the good shepherd' (John 10) builds on Ezekiel 34, and Revelation borrows many of Ezekiel's images: the living creatures, the measuring of the temple, the river of life.

books.means: Named after Daniel.
books.kind: Narrative and apocalyptic visions; 2:4–7:28 is written in Aramaic
books.author: Daniel, taken to Babylon as a young man in 605 BC
books.authorMeans: Daniel means 'God is my judge'.
books.authorNote: Many scholars date the book to about 165 BC, during the persecution under Antiochus IV, reading chapters 7–12 as written close to the events they describe. Jesus refers to 'the prophet Daniel' (Matthew 24:15).
books.to: Jews in exile and under foreign rule
books.summary: Daniel and his friends were taken from Jerusalem to serve in Babylon's royal court. Chapters 1–6 are stories of faithfulness under pressure: refusing the king's food, interpreting Nebuchadnezzar's dreams, the fiery furnace, the writing on the wall, the lions' den. Chapters 7–12 are visions of beasts and kingdoms rising and falling until 'one like a son of man' receives an everlasting kingdom from the Ancient of Days. The message to God's people under foreign rule: God rules over empires, and his kingdom will outlast them all.
books.fits: Jesus' favorite name for himself, 'the Son of Man', comes from Daniel 7, and Revelation draws heavily on Daniel's visions.

books.means: Named after the prophet Hosea.
books.author: Hosea son of Beeri, a prophet to the northern kingdom
books.authorMeans: Hosea means 'salvation'.
books.to: The northern kingdom (Israel, often called Ephraim)
books.summary: God told Hosea to marry Gomer, who would be unfaithful to him, and his broken marriage became a living picture of Israel's unfaithfulness in worshiping Baal. Their children's names announce judgment, yet Hosea is told to love his wife again and buy her back. The rest of the book alternates accusation and tender appeal: Israel lacks 'knowledge of God', trusts in Egypt and Assyria, and will fall. Yet God cries, 'How can I give you up?' and promises to heal their waywardness.
themes: God's loyal love for an unfaithful people
books.fits: Jesus twice quoted 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice' (Matthew 9:13; 12:7), and Matthew saw 'Out of Egypt I called my son' fulfilled in him.

books.means: Named after the prophet Joel.
books.author: Joel son of Pethuel
books.authorMeans: Joel means 'the LORD is God'.
books.date: Uncertain; suggestions range from the 800s BC to after the exile
books.summary: A devastating locust plague becomes Joel's picture of the coming 'day of the LORD'. He calls everyone, from elders and priests to a bride and groom, to fast and return to God, who is 'gracious and compassionate'. Then the tone turns: God will repay the years the locusts ate, pour out his Spirit on all people, judge the nations, and dwell in Zion.
themes: The Spirit poured out on all people
books.fits: Peter quoted Joel 2 to explain Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21), and Paul cites 'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved' (Romans 10:13).

books.means: Named after the prophet Amos.
books.author: Amos, a shepherd and fig-tree farmer from Tekoa in Judah
books.authorMeans: Amos probably means 'burden-bearer'.
books.summary: Amos, a farmer from Judah, was sent north to Israel in a time of wealth and security. He began by condemning the surrounding nations, and then turned the same judgment on Israel: for selling the needy for a pair of sandals, crushing the poor, and holding religious festivals God hates. Five visions show judgment coming, and the priest Amaziah tells him to go home. The book ends with a promise that God will restore David's fallen shelter.
outline: Judgment on the nations and Israel
books.fits: James quoted Amos 9:11–12 at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:16–17) to show that Gentiles belong in God's people.

books.means: Named after the prophet Obadiah.
books.author: Obadiah; nothing else is known of him
books.authorMeans: Obadiah means 'servant of the LORD'.
books.date: Probably soon after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC
books.summary: The shortest book in the Old Testament is a single message against Edom, the nation descended from Esau, which gloated and joined in when Babylon sacked Jerusalem. Edom's pride in its mountain strongholds will not save it: 'As you have done, it will be done to you.' The book ends looking ahead: 'the kingdom will be the LORD's.'
themes: Judgment on those who harm God's people
books.fits: The last chapter in a long rivalry that began with Jacob and Esau (Genesis 25–27).

books.means: Named after Jonah.
books.author: Unknown; the story is about Jonah son of Amittai
books.authorMeans: Jonah means 'dove'.
books.date: Jonah prophesied under Jeroboam II, about 780–750 BC (2 Kings 14:25)
books.summary: Told to preach against Nineveh, Assyria's great city, Jonah runs the other way. A storm, praying sailors and a great fish bring him back, and from inside the fish he prays a psalm of thanks. His five-word message in Nineveh (in Hebrew) brings city-wide repentance, and God relents. Jonah is furious: he knew God was gracious and compassionate. He sulks under a plant that withers, and the book ends with God's unanswered question: shouldn't I care about this great city?
books.fits: Jesus pointed to 'the sign of Jonah' as a picture of his three days in the grave (Matthew 12:39–41).

books.means: Named after the prophet Micah.
books.author: Micah of Moresheth, a country prophet and contemporary of Isaiah
books.authorMeans: Micah means 'Who is like the LORD?'
books.summary: Micah preached to both capitals, Samaria and Jerusalem. He condemns land-grabbing, corrupt judges, and priests and prophets who work for pay, and he predicts that Jerusalem will be plowed like a field. Each section turns from judgment to hope: the nations streaming to God's mountain, and a ruler from little Bethlehem who will shepherd his flock. In a courtroom scene God sums up what he requires: to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly with him.
books.fits: The priests quoted Micah 5:2 to Herod as the birthplace of the Messiah (Matthew 2:6). Jeremiah 26:18 quotes Micah, one prophet citing another.

books.means: Named after the prophet Nahum.
books.author: Nahum of Elkosh
books.authorMeans: Nahum means 'comfort'.
books.summary: About a century after Jonah, Nineveh had returned to cruelty, and Assyria had destroyed the northern kingdom and terrorized Judah. Nahum announces its fall in vivid war poetry. The LORD is slow to anger, but he will not leave the guilty unpunished, and he is a refuge for those who trust him. Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC.
themes: Slow to anger, great in power
books.fits: The sequel to Jonah: mercy offered, then judgment when evil returns.

books.means: Named after the prophet Habakkuk.
books.kind: Prophecy: dialogue with God and a psalm
books.author: Habakkuk; nothing else is known of him
books.authorMeans: Habakkuk may come from a word for 'embrace', or the name of a garden plant.
books.summary: Habakkuk argues with God. Why does God tolerate violence in Judah? God answers that he is raising up the Babylonians to judge them. But they are worse than us, the prophet objects. God's second answer: the vision will come at the right time, the proud will fall, and 'the righteous will live by faith'. The book ends with a psalm: even if the fig tree does not bud and the fields produce no food, 'yet I will rejoice in the LORD.'
books.fits: Paul built his teaching on faith on Habakkuk 2:4 (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11), and Hebrews 10:38 quotes it too.

books.means: Named after the prophet Zephaniah.
books.author: Zephaniah, a descendant of King Hezekiah
books.authorMeans: Zephaniah means 'the LORD hides' or 'the LORD treasures'.
books.summary: Zephaniah preached early in King Josiah's reign. The day of the LORD is near, a day of wrath that will sweep away idolatry in Judah and among the nations. A humble remnant will be sheltered. The book ends with one of Scripture's most tender pictures: God rejoicing over his people with singing.
books.fits: Probably preached before Josiah's reforms of 622 BC, it may have helped prepare for them.

books.means: Named after the prophet Haggai.
books.author: Haggai
books.authorMeans: Haggai means 'festal', perhaps because he was born on a feast day.
books.summary: Sixteen years after the exiles returned, the temple still lay unfinished while people paneled their own houses. Haggai's four messages, all dated to 520 BC, tell them to give careful thought to their ways: their harvests fail because they neglect God's house. Governor Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua lead the people back to work. God promises his Spirit, greater glory for this house, and a special place for Zerubbabel as his signet ring.
books.fits: Read with Ezra 5–6 and Zechariah. Hebrews 12:26 quotes the promise that God will shake the heavens and the earth.

books.means: Named after the prophet Zechariah.
books.author: Zechariah son of Berekiah, a priest and prophet
books.authorMeans: Zechariah means 'the LORD remembers'.
books.authorNote: Some scholars think chapters 9–14 come from a later writer.
books.date: Beginning in 520 BC; chapters 9–14 perhaps later in his life
books.summary: Zechariah began preaching alongside Haggai to encourage the temple builders. Eight night visions (horsemen, horns, a measuring line, a lampstand, a flying scroll and more) assure them that God is jealous for Jerusalem and will remove its guilt. The later chapters look far ahead: a king coming humble and riding on a donkey, a shepherd valued at thirty pieces of silver, one 'they have pierced', a fountain to cleanse sin, and the LORD as king over the whole earth.
themes: 'Return to me, and I will return to you' (1:3)
'Not by might nor by power, but by my Spirit' (4:6)
books.fits: The Gospels quote Zechariah often in the last week of Jesus' life: the entry into Jerusalem, the thirty pieces of silver, the struck shepherd, the pierced one.

books.means: Named after its author, or from its key word: Malachi means 'my messenger' (3:1).
books.author: Malachi
books.authorMeans: 'My messenger'. It may be a title rather than a personal name.
books.summary: Malachi speaks to a disillusioned community a few generations after the return. In a series of disputes, God makes a statement, the people object ('How?'), and God answers. He exposes blemished sacrifices, careless priests, broken marriages, withheld tithes and cynical talk. God promises to send his messenger to prepare the way and then come suddenly to his temple, and to send the prophet Elijah before the great day of the LORD.
outline: Broken faith and the coming messenger
The day of the LORD and Elijah
books.fits: The last of the prophets before about 400 years of silence. The New Testament opens with John the Baptist, whom Jesus called the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14).

books.means: Named after its traditional author.
books.kind: Gospel: an ancient biography of Jesus
books.author: Matthew (also called Levi), a tax collector who became one of the twelve apostles
books.authorMeans: Matthew means 'gift of the LORD'.
books.authorNote: The Gospel doesn't name its author; the early church was unanimous that it was Matthew.
books.to: Jewish Christians, probably in Syria or Palestine
books.summary: Matthew presents Jesus as the Messiah promised in Israel's Scriptures, the son of David and son of Abraham. Again and again he notes that something happened 'to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet'. The story is built around five great blocks of teaching: the Sermon on the Mount, the sending of the Twelve, the parables of the kingdom, life together as disciples, and the end of the age. Many see these as echoing the five books of Moses. Matthew stresses the kingdom of heaven, Jesus' authority as teacher, and conflict with the religious leaders, and he ends with the risen Jesus sending his disciples to make disciples of all nations.
books.fits: It comes first because it binds the Testaments together, opening with a family tree from Abraham through David to Jesus.

books.means: Named after its traditional author.
books.kind: Gospel: an ancient biography of Jesus
books.author: John Mark, a companion of Paul, Barnabas and Peter. Early tradition (Papias, about AD 110) says he wrote down Peter's preaching
books.authorMeans: Mark is the Latin name Marcus; his Jewish name, John, means 'the LORD is gracious' (Acts 12:12).
books.summary: Mark is the shortest and fastest-moving Gospel; 'immediately' is one of its favorite words. It skips Jesus' birth and opens with John the Baptist. The first half shows Jesus' authority over demons, disease, nature and sin, and keeps raising the question 'Who is this?' Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi is the turning point. From there Jesus heads for Jerusalem, three times predicting his death, and nearly a third of the book covers the last week. The Son of Man came 'not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.'
themes: Following Jesus means taking up the cross
books.fits: Most scholars think Mark was the first Gospel written and that Matthew and Luke used it. The earliest manuscripts end at 16:8; verses 9–20 were added later.

books.means: Named after its traditional author.
books.kind: Gospel: an ancient biography of Jesus, the first of a two-part work
books.author: Luke, a doctor and Paul's traveling companion, who also wrote Acts
books.authorMeans: Loukas is a Greek name, probably short for the Latin Lucanus; its meaning is uncertain.
books.to: Theophilus, a Gentile believer, and readers like him
books.summary: Luke wrote 'an orderly account' for Theophilus after investigating carefully. His Gospel has the fullest birth story, with songs from Mary, Zechariah and Simeon, and pays special attention to the poor, women, Samaritans, tax collectors and sinners. A long middle section follows Jesus' journey to Jerusalem and includes parables found only here: the good Samaritan, the lost son, the Pharisee and the tax collector. Luke stresses prayer, the Holy Spirit and joy, and ends with the risen Jesus explaining the Scriptures to his disciples.
books.fits: Volume one of a two-part work; Acts continues the story. Together they make up over a quarter of the New Testament.

books.means: Named after its traditional author.
books.kind: Gospel: an ancient biography of Jesus
books.author: John son of Zebedee, 'the disciple whom Jesus loved'
books.authorMeans: John means 'the LORD is gracious'.
books.authorNote: The Gospel names its source as 'the disciple whom Jesus loved' (21:24). Early tradition identifies him with the apostle John; some scholars think he was a different disciple.
books.to: Believers, and seekers ("that you may believe")
books.summary: John opens before creation: 'In the beginning was the Word.' Unlike the other three, it is built around seven signs, from water turned to wine to Lazarus raised, and long conversations and speeches, including the 'I am' sayings: the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life. The second half slows down to the final week, with Jesus' farewell teaching on the Spirit, love and abiding in him (13–17). John states his purpose plainly: these are written 'that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.'
books.fits: Matthew, Mark and Luke share much material; most of John's is his own. Early Christians called it 'the spiritual gospel'.

books.means: Short for 'The Acts of the Apostles', a title from the second century.
books.author: Luke, as volume two of his work (1:1)
books.authorMeans: Loukas is a Greek name, probably short for the Latin Lucanus.
books.to: Theophilus, as the sequel to Luke
books.summary: Acts continues what Jesus 'began to do and to teach' through his Spirit-filled followers. Jesus promises they will be his witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth (1:8), and the book follows that outline. The Spirit comes at Pentecost and the Jerusalem church grows despite persecution. Stephen is martyred, the gospel reaches Samaria and an Ethiopian official, Saul the persecutor is converted, and Peter sees Gentiles receive the Spirit. The second half follows Paul's three missionary journeys, his arrest, and his voyage to Rome, where the book ends with him preaching 'with all boldness and without hindrance'.
themes: The Holy Spirit empowers the church
Witnesses to the ends of the earth
Jews and Gentiles in one people
outline: Paul's arrest and voyage to Rome
books.fits: The bridge between the Gospels and the letters; most of Paul's letters fit into its story.

books.means: Named for its readers, the church in Rome.
books.author: The apostle Paul
books.authorMeans: Paul (Latin Paulus) means 'small'. His Hebrew name, Saul, means 'asked for'.
books.to: The church in Rome, which Paul had not yet visited
books.summary: Paul's fullest explanation of the gospel, written to a church he hoped would support his mission to Spain. All have sinned, Gentiles and Jews alike, and all are justified freely by God's grace through faith in Christ's sacrifice, just as Abraham was. Chapters 5–8 trace the new life this brings: peace with God, freedom from sin's rule and the law's condemnation, life in the Spirit, and the certainty that nothing can separate us from God's love. Chapters 9–11 wrestle with Israel's place in God's plan, and 12–16 turn to living sacrifices, love, government, and welcoming one another across differences.
themes: Jews and Gentiles in God's plan
outline: New life in Christ and the Spirit
books.fits: First of the letters because it is the longest. It has been at the center of turning points in church history, from Augustine to Luther and Wesley.

books.means: Named for its readers, the church in Corinth.
books.author: The apostle Paul
books.authorMeans: Paul (Latin Paulus) means 'small'. His Hebrew name, Saul, means 'asked for'.
books.to: The church in Corinth, which Paul had planted
books.summary: Corinth was a wealthy, cosmopolitan port, and the church there was gifted but divided and proud. Paul addresses factions loyal to different teachers, a case of incest, lawsuits between believers, sexual immorality, marriage and singleness, food offered to idols, order in worship and the Lord's Supper, and spiritual gifts. In the middle of the discussion of gifts he writes the great chapter on love (13), and he ends with the New Testament's fullest teaching on the resurrection (15).
books.fits: Paul wrote at least four letters to Corinth; two survive. This one shows the gospel applied to messy church life.

books.means: Named for its readers, the church in Corinth.
books.author: The apostle Paul
books.authorMeans: Paul (Latin Paulus) means 'small'. His Hebrew name, Saul, means 'asked for'.
books.summary: Paul's most personal letter. After a painful visit and a severe letter, he writes with relief that the church has repented, but also defends his ministry against 'super-apostles' who mocked his weakness. He describes the ministry of the new covenant, treasure in jars of clay, becoming a new creation, and the ministry of reconciliation. Two chapters encourage generous giving for the poor in Jerusalem. He ends by boasting in his weaknesses: 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.'
books.fits: Shows the cost of ministry and the shape of Christian leadership: power through weakness, like the cross.

books.means: Named for its readers, the churches in Galatia (central Turkey).
books.author: The apostle Paul
books.authorMeans: Paul (Latin Paulus) means 'small'. His Hebrew name, Saul, means 'asked for'.
books.date: About AD 48–49 if before the Jerusalem council; otherwise the mid-50s
books.summary: Paul's sharpest letter. Teachers had told Gentile believers in Galatia they must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong to God's people. Paul defends his calling as an apostle, recounts confronting Peter at Antioch, and argues from Abraham's faith that we are justified by faith in Christ, not by works of the law. In Christ there is neither Jew nor Gentile, slave nor free, male nor female. Freedom is not license: walk by the Spirit and bear his fruit.
books.fits: Possibly Paul's earliest letter. The issue it fights over was settled at the Jerusalem council in Acts 15.

books.means: Named for its readers in Ephesus.
books.author: The apostle Paul
books.authorMeans: Paul (Latin Paulus) means 'small'. His Hebrew name, Saul, means 'asked for'.
books.authorNote: The words 'in Ephesus' are missing from some of the earliest manuscripts, so it may have been a circular letter for several churches. Some scholars think a follower of Paul wrote it.
books.date: About AD 60–62, from prison in Rome
books.to: The church in Ephesus and probably nearby churches
books.summary: Written from prison, Ephesians has no crisis to fix; it lifts the eyes. Chapters 1–3 praise God for every spiritual blessing in Christ: chosen, redeemed, sealed by the Spirit, saved by grace through faith, and, Jew and Gentile alike, made one new humanity, a temple where God lives. Chapters 4–6 work it out: unity and growth in the body, the new self, walking in love and light, households shaped by Christ's love, and standing firm in the armor of God.
books.fits: One of the four 'prison letters', with Philippians, Colossians and Philemon. It shares much with Colossians.

books.means: Named for its readers, the church in Philippi in Macedonia (northern Greece).
books.author: The apostle Paul
books.authorMeans: Paul (Latin Paulus) means 'small'. His Hebrew name, Saul, means 'asked for'.
books.date: About AD 61, from prison in Rome
books.summary: A thank-you letter from prison to Paul's dearest church, which had sent him a gift. Despite chains and rivals, Paul rejoices that Christ is preached: 'to live is Christ and to die is gain.' He urges unity and humility by quoting the great hymn of Christ, who emptied himself, became obedient to death on a cross, and was exalted. He counts all his credentials as loss compared with knowing Christ, presses on toward the goal, and has learned to be content in every circumstance.
books.fits: The church in Philippi began with Lydia and the jailer in Acts 16.

books.means: Named for its readers, the church in Colossae (western Turkey).
books.author: The apostle Paul
books.authorMeans: Paul (Latin Paulus) means 'small'. His Hebrew name, Saul, means 'asked for'.
books.to: The church in Colossae, which Paul had never visited
books.summary: The church in Colossae was being drawn toward a teaching that mixed special knowledge, the worship of angels, and rules about food and festivals. Paul answers by exalting Christ: the image of the invisible God, creator and sustainer of all things, in whom all the fullness of God lives in bodily form. Believers have been raised with him, so they need nothing added. They should set their minds on things above and put on the new self, with practical teaching for households.
books.fits: Sent along with Philemon, whose slave Onesimus carried both letters (4:9).

books.means: Named for its readers, the church in Thessalonica in Macedonia.
books.author: The apostle Paul
books.authorMeans: Paul (Latin Paulus) means 'small'. His Hebrew name, Saul, means 'asked for'.
books.summary: Paul had to leave Thessalonica after only a few weeks. When Timothy brought news that the new believers were standing firm under persecution, Paul wrote with warmth and relief. He recalls his time among them, urges holy living and love, and answers a worry: what happens to believers who have died? They will rise first when the Lord returns, and those still alive will join them. The day will come like a thief in the night, so stay awake.
books.fits: Probably one of the earliest New Testament writings. The church's founding is told in Acts 17.

books.means: Named for its readers, the church in Thessalonica.
books.author: The apostle Paul
books.authorMeans: Paul (Latin Paulus) means 'small'. His Hebrew name, Saul, means 'asked for'.
books.authorNote: Some scholars question whether Paul wrote it because its view of the end differs in emphasis from 1 Thessalonians.
books.summary: A short follow-up after some in Thessalonica decided the day of the Lord had already come, and some stopped working. Paul encourages them under persecution, explains that 'the man of lawlessness' must appear first, and tells the idle: 'The one who is unwilling to work shall not eat.'
books.fits: Read with 1 Thessalonians; together they are Paul's main teaching on the Lord's return.

books.means: Named for its reader, Timothy.
books.author: The apostle Paul
books.authorMeans: Paul (Latin Paulus) means 'small'. His Hebrew name, Saul, means 'asked for'.
books.authorNote: Many scholars question whether Paul wrote the Pastoral Letters (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) because their vocabulary and church setting differ from his other letters. The letters themselves claim Paul, and the church received them as his from early on.
books.to: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, leading the church in Ephesus
books.summary: Paul left Timothy in Ephesus to deal with false teachers. The letter is a guide to church life: guard sound teaching, pray for everyone, choose overseers and deacons of proven character, care for widows, beware the love of money. It also has personal charges to Timothy: don't let anyone look down on you because you are young; set an example; fight the good fight of the faith.
books.fits: Timothy's name means 'honoring God'. He was half Jewish, half Greek, and joined Paul in Acts 16.

books.means: Named for its reader, Timothy.
books.author: The apostle Paul
books.authorMeans: Paul (Latin Paulus) means 'small'. His Hebrew name, Saul, means 'asked for'.
books.authorNote: Many scholars question whether Paul wrote the Pastoral Letters (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) because their vocabulary and church setting differ from his other letters. The letters themselves claim Paul, and the church received them as his from early on.
books.date: About AD 67, from prison in Rome, shortly before Paul's execution
books.summary: Paul's last letter, written from a Roman prison as he expects to die. Most have deserted him. He urges Timothy not to be ashamed, to guard the gospel and entrust it to faithful people, to endure hardship like a soldier, and to preach the word in season and out of season, because all Scripture is God-breathed. 'I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.'
books.fits: Paul's farewell, like Moses' in Deuteronomy and Peter's in 2 Peter.

books.means: Named for its reader, Titus.
books.author: The apostle Paul
books.authorMeans: Paul (Latin Paulus) means 'small'. His Hebrew name, Saul, means 'asked for'.
books.authorNote: Many scholars question whether Paul wrote the Pastoral Letters (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) because their vocabulary and church setting differ from his other letters. The letters themselves claim Paul, and the church received them as his from early on.
books.to: Titus, a Gentile co-worker leading churches in Crete
books.summary: Paul left Titus in Crete to appoint elders and correct false teachers in a culture known for its vices. The letter ties belief to daily life: leaders of good character, sound teaching for each group in the church, and good works that make the gospel attractive. Twice Paul sums up the gospel: the grace of God has appeared, teaching us to live godly lives, and God saved us 'not because of righteous things we had done, but because of his mercy'.
books.fits: Titus was a Greek believer whom Paul took to Jerusalem as a test case (Galatians 2:1–3).

books.means: Named for its reader, Philemon.
books.author: The apostle Paul
books.authorMeans: Paul (Latin Paulus) means 'small'. His Hebrew name, Saul, means 'asked for'.
books.to: Philemon, a believer in Colossae, and the church in his house
books.summary: A personal letter about Onesimus, Philemon's slave, who had run away and become a Christian through Paul in prison. Paul sends him back, asking Philemon to welcome him 'no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a dear brother', and offers to pay anything owed himself. Onesimus means 'useful', and Paul plays on it: he was once useless to you, but now he is useful.
books.fits: Philemon means 'loving' or 'affectionate'. Delivered with Colossians (Colossians 4:9).

books.means: Named for its readers, Jewish (Hebrew) believers.
books.kind: A sermon sent as a letter
books.author: Unknown
books.authorNote: Paul, Barnabas, Apollos and Luke have all been suggested. The early scholar Origen said, 'Who wrote it, only God knows.'
books.date: Before AD 70, since the temple sacrifices seem still to be going on
books.to: Jewish Christians tempted to turn back
books.summary: Hebrews is a sermon written to Jewish believers under pressure to turn back. Its argument is that Jesus is better: better than angels, than Moses, than Joshua's rest, and than the priests descended from Aaron. He is a high priest in the order of Melchizedek who offered himself once for all and opened a new and living way into God's presence. Woven through the argument are urgent warnings not to drift. The great list of the faithful in chapter 11 leads into a call to run the race with eyes fixed on Jesus.
books.fits: The New Testament's key to Leviticus: it shows how the tabernacle, priesthood and sacrifices point to Christ.

books.means: Named after its author.
books.author: James, the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church
books.authorMeans: James is the Greek form of Jacob, 'he grasps the heel'.
books.date: About AD 45–49, possibly the earliest New Testament book
books.summary: James reads like Proverbs for the New Testament: short, direct teaching for scattered Jewish believers. Trials produce perseverance; ask God for wisdom; be doers of the word, not hearers only. Don't favor the rich; faith without deeds is dead; tame the tongue; seek wisdom from above; submit to God; don't boast about tomorrow; and pray, because the prayer of a righteous person is powerful.
books.fits: Luther once called it 'an epistle of straw', but James and Paul agree. Paul says we are saved by faith, not works; James says the faith that saves will show itself in works.

books.means: Named after its author.
books.author: The apostle Peter, with help from Silas (5:12)
books.authorMeans: Peter (Greek Petros) means 'rock', as does his Aramaic name Cephas. His birth name was Simon, 'he has heard'.
books.date: About AD 62–64, from Rome (which he calls 'Babylon')
books.summary: Peter writes to believers across Asia Minor who are suffering as outsiders. He reminds them of a living hope through Christ's resurrection, an inheritance that can never perish, and who they now are: a chosen people and a royal priesthood. They are to live as foreigners and exiles, doing good, honoring authorities, and serving one another in households and marriages, following Christ's example when they suffer unjustly. To suffer for doing good is to share in Christ's sufferings, and glory follows.
books.fits: Peter's teaching echoes Jesus' words to him in John 21: 'Feed my sheep' (compare 5:2).

books.means: Named after its author.
books.author: The apostle Peter
books.authorMeans: Peter means 'rock'.
books.authorNote: Its authorship is the most debated in the New Testament, because of differences in style from 1 Peter and its close overlap with Jude. Peter could have used a different secretary.
books.date: About AD 65–68, shortly before Peter's death
books.summary: Peter's farewell, written knowing his death is near. He urges believers to grow in goodness, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness and love. He recalls witnessing Jesus' glory at the Transfiguration, warns against false teachers driven by greed and immorality, and answers scoffers who ask where Christ's promised return is: with the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and he is patient, not wanting anyone to perish.
books.fits: Chapter 2 closely parallels Jude. 3:16 is the earliest place Paul's letters are called Scripture.

books.means: Named after its traditional author.
books.author: The apostle John (traditional); the letter doesn't name him
books.authorMeans: John means 'the LORD is gracious'.
books.summary: John writes as a pastor to churches shaken by teachers who had left them and denied that Jesus came in the flesh. He gives tests so believers can know they have eternal life: walking in the light, keeping God's commands, loving one another, and confessing that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh. God is light and God is love; if we confess our sins, he is faithful to forgive.
books.fits: Shares its language with John's Gospel: light, life, love, truth, abiding.

books.means: Named after its traditional author.
books.author: 'The elder', traditionally the apostle John
books.authorMeans: John means 'the LORD is gracious'.
books.to: 'The lady chosen by God and her children', probably a church and its members
books.summary: A short note urging a church to keep loving one another and walking in the truth, and not to welcome traveling teachers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.
books.fits: A short companion to 1 John, dealing with the same false teachers.

books.means: Named after its traditional author.
books.author: 'The elder', traditionally the apostle John
books.authorMeans: John means 'the LORD is gracious'.
books.summary: A personal letter praising Gaius for welcoming traveling missionaries, rebuking Diotrephes, 'who loves to be first' and refuses them, and recommending Demetrius.
books.fits: A glimpse of how early missionaries traveled and depended on local hospitality.

books.means: Named after its author.
books.author: Jude, brother of James and of Jesus
books.authorMeans: Jude is the Greek form of Judah, 'praise'.
books.summary: Jude meant to write about the salvation they share, but instead urges his readers to contend for the faith, because ungodly people have slipped in, turning God's grace into an excuse for immorality. He piles up examples of judgment (Israel in the wilderness, fallen angels, Sodom, Cain, Balaam, Korah) and quotes the Jewish book of 1 Enoch. Then he turns to the faithful: build yourselves up, pray in the Spirit, show mercy. It closes with one of the New Testament's best-known blessings.
themes: God is able to keep you
books.fits: Much of it is shared with 2 Peter 2.

books.means: Greek Apokalypsis, 'unveiling'. It is 'the revelation of Jesus Christ' (1:1); the singular, not 'Revelations'.
books.kind: Apocalyptic prophecy in the form of a letter
books.author: John, writing in exile on the island of Patmos; traditionally the apostle
books.authorMeans: John means 'the LORD is gracious'.
books.authorNote: Some early and modern scholars think this John was a different John from the apostle, because its Greek differs from the Gospel's.
books.date: About AD 95, under the emperor Domitian (some date it to the late 60s)
books.summary: Revelation records visions given to John in exile on Patmos, written to seven churches in Asia under pressure to compromise with Rome. Jesus speaks to each church, then John is taken up to the throne room of heaven, where the Lamb who was slain takes the sealed scroll. Seven seals, seven trumpets and seven bowls of judgment unfold in symbolic visions of the conflict between God and the dragon, the beasts and 'Babylon'. Babylon falls, Christ rides out as King of kings, Satan is defeated, the dead are judged, and the book ends with a new heaven and new earth where God lives with his people and wipes away every tear.
themes: Christ wins as the slain Lamb
books.fits: The Bible's last word mirrors its first: Genesis begins with creation, the garden and the tree of life; Revelation ends with new creation, a garden city and the tree of life.
